summary.text: Gambler's ruin is the fact that a gambler playing a game that is not in their favor will eventually go bankrupt, no matter what betting system they use.
Even in a fair game, a gambler with limited money who keeps playing against an opponent with unlimited money will eventually go broke.
The idea comes from a theorem by Christiaan Huygens and led to important advances in the mathematical theory of probability.

facts.label: Core claim
facts.value: A non-positive expected value game ends in bankruptcy, whatever the betting system

facts.label: Modeled as
facts.value: A random walk on the real number line

facts.label: Origin
facts.value: A general theorem by Christiaan Huygens

facts.label: What Huygens' theorem finds
facts.value: Each player's chance of winning a series of bets until one is wiped out

facts.label: Small stake disadvantage
facts.value: Even with equal odds, the player starting with fewer pennies is likelier to fail

items.prompt: A gambler with a limited bankroll plays a perfectly fair game, every night, against an opponent with unlimited money. What does the theory say happens eventually?

options.label: The gambler goes broke
The gambler ends up well ahead
The results balance out, so the gambler stays afloat
It depends on how big the first bet is

items.explain: A persistent gambler with finite wealth, playing a fair game against an opponent with infinite wealth, will eventually and inevitably go broke.

items.prompt: Your friend invents a clever betting system for a game that is slightly stacked against him. Will the system save him from going broke in the long run?

options.label: Yes, any careful system beats a small disadvantage
Only if he changes the bet size after every round
Yes, as long as he starts with enough money
No, he will eventually go bankrupt whatever system he uses

items.explain: Gambler's ruin says a player in a game with non-positive expected value eventually goes bankrupt regardless of their betting system.

items.prompt: Is a gambler who plays a game tilted against them any better off in the long run than one who plays a perfectly fair game?

options.label: Yes, because a tilted game ends sooner and cuts losses
No, their eventual fate cannot be better, so they go broke too
Yes, because they are more careful with each bet
No, but only if the casino has unlimited money

items.explain: The eventual fate of a player at a game with negative expected value cannot be better than that of a player at a fair game, so they go broke as well.

items.prompt: Two friends flip a fair coin, and the loser of each flip hands the winner one penny. One starts with 3 pennies, the other with 50. Who is more likely to end up with nothing?

options.label: The one with 50, since they have more to lose
Neither, since the coin is fair to both
The one with 3, since a short losing run wipes them out
Each is equally likely, since each flip is 50-50

items.explain: Even with equal odds on each flip, the player who starts with fewer pennies is more likely to fail.

items.prompt: A gambler raises each bet after a win and never lowers it after a loss, and each bet has a favorable expected value. What outcome is virtually certain over time?

options.label: The bets stay profitable, so the bankroll grows steadily
The gambler stabilizes at a constant bankroll
The gambler is protected, since each bet favors them
The gambler eventually goes broke

items.explain: Such a persistent gambler will eventually go broke, even if each bet has a positive expected value.

items.prompt: Suppose you know each of two players' starting money, and each bet has the same chance of being won. Huygens's theorem lets you work out what?

options.label: How long a single bet will take to settle
How much each player should wager on every bet
Which player is the more skilled gambler
Each player's chance of winning the whole series of bets

items.explain: The theorem computes the probability of each player winning a series of bets that continues until one player's entire stake is lost.
